### 8.2 By lab

#### Anthropic

Anthropic's practice has moved from LLM-driven orchestration toward code-driven orchestration. Claude Code now offers four tiers: subagents, experimental agent teams, dynamic workflows, and (in Anthropic's own projects) orchestrator-free swarms. Anthropic repeatedly warns that multi-agent setups pay off only for parallelizable, read-heavy or independently verifiable work.

**Multi-agent research system ("How we built our multi-agent research system", Jun 13, 2025)** — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- *Architecture:* orchestrator-worker. A lead agent (Claude Opus 4) plans, saves the plan to memory, spawns subagents (Claude Sonnet 4) that search in parallel with interleaved thinking, and decides whether more research is needed. A separate **CitationAgent** then places citations against the source documents.
- *Result:* the Opus 4 lead with Sonnet 4 subagents beat single-agent Opus 4 by **90.2%** on Anthropic's internal research eval. No per-task breakdown was given and the eval set is not published.
- *Variance:* on BrowseComp, three factors explained **95%** of performance variance. **Token usage alone explained 80%**; the other two were number of tool calls and model choice. Upgrading to Sonnet 4 gained more than doubling the token budget on Sonnet 3.7.
- *Cost:* agents use about **4x** the tokens of chat and multi-agent systems about **15x**. The task value has to justify this.
- *Effort scaling, written into the prompt:*
  - simple fact-finding: 1 agent, 3–10 tool calls
  - direct comparisons: 2–4 subagents, 10–15 calls each
  - complex research: more than 10 subagents with divided responsibilities
- *Parallelism:* the lead spawns **3–5 subagents at once**, and each subagent uses **3+ tools in parallel**. This cut research time **by up to 90%** on complex queries.
- *Prompting principles:*
  1. Simulate agents step by step with the exact prompts and tools.
  2. Give the lead detailed delegation briefs: **objective, output format, guidance on tools and sources, clear task boundaries**. Without them, subagents duplicate work or leave gaps. A vague brief such as "research the semiconductor shortage" led subagents to duplicate each other's work.
  3. Encode the effort-scaling rules.
  4. Make tool design and selection explicit: distinct purposes, clear descriptions, specialized tools preferred.
  5. Let Claude improve its own prompts and tools. A tool-testing agent rewrote a flawed MCP tool description and **cut task completion time by 40%** for later agents.
  6. Start wide, then narrow.
  7. Use extended thinking for planning and interleaved thinking after tool results.
  8. Parallelize.
- *Evaluation:* start with **about 20 real-usage queries**, because early changes have large effect sizes; one prompt tweak moved success from 30% to 80% — [evals notes citing Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system). The LLM-as-judge rubric covers factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality and tool efficiency. A single call returning a 0.0–1.0 score plus pass/fail was the most consistent and closest to human judgment. Stateful agents are judged on **end state**, not per step. Human testers still caught failures automation missed, such as SEO content farms ranked above authoritative sources; source-quality heuristics in the prompt fixed it.
- *Production reliability:*
  - Agents are stateful, so errors compound. The system **resumes from where the error occurred** instead of restarting, using regular checkpoints and retry logic. Agents are told when a tool is failing so they can adapt.
  - Full production tracing is in place. It monitors "agent decision patterns and interaction structures" but not conversation contents, for privacy.
  - **Rainbow deployments** shift traffic gradually from the old version to the new one while both run, so running agents are not broken mid-flight.
  - Synchronous execution is a bottleneck: the lead waits for each batch, and subagents cannot steer or coordinate with each other. Async execution was planned. The notes found no follow-up confirming it shipped.
- *Long-horizon context:* the plan is saved to memory because context beyond **200k tokens** is truncated. Completed phases are summarized into external memory, and fresh subagents with clean contexts are spawned as limits approach. Subagents can write outputs to an **external artifact system or filesystem** and pass **lightweight references** back. This avoids a "game of telephone" and saves tokens.
- *Poor fit:* tasks where all agents need the same context, tasks with many inter-agent dependencies, and tasks with few parallelizable subtasks, "e.g., most coding tasks."

**Context engineering post (Sep 29, 2025)** — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)
- Sub-agents explore with tens of thousands of tokens but return condensed summaries, "often 1,000–2,000 tokens."
- The Claude Agent SDK post (same date) says subagents "use their own isolated context windows, and only send relevant information back." It also calls LLM-as-judge verification "generally not a very robust method", ranking it after rules/linting and visual feedback (Playwright MCP) — [Claude blog: Building agents with the Claude Agent SDK](https://claude.com/blog/building-agents-with-the-claude-agent-sdk).

**Initializer plus coding agent ("Effective harnesses for long-running agents", Nov 26, 2025, Justin Young)** — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents)
- Two-agent sequential design. An **initializer agent** sets up the environment on the first run. A **coding agent** makes incremental progress in each later fresh-context session. The two differ *only in the initial user prompt*; system prompt, tools and harness are identical. Model: Opus 4.5 on the Claude Agent SDK.
- State passes between sessions as files: `init.sh`, `claude-progress.txt`, git commits with descriptive messages, and a JSON feature list. In the claude.ai-clone experiment the list held more than 200 features, all initially failing, each with `category`, `description`, `steps` and `passes`. Agents may only flip `passes`. JSON was chosen because the model is less likely to edit it inappropriately than Markdown. The prompt says: "It is unacceptable to remove or edit tests because this could lead to missing or buggy functionality."
- Coding-session start ritual: `pwd`; read git logs and progress files; read the feature list and pick the highest-priority failing feature; run `init.sh` and a basic end-to-end test before new work. One feature per session, ending with a commit and a progress update.
- Failure modes addressed: one-shotting (fix: one feature per session); declaring victory early (fix: feature list); marking features done without end-to-end tests (fix: Puppeteer MCP browser testing "as a human user would"); wasted startup time (fix: `init.sh`). "Compaction isn't sufficient" because it "doesn't always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent."
- The post says it is "still unclear whether a single, general-purpose coding agent performs best." Specialized testing, QA or cleanup agents are listed as future work.
- Open reference implementation: `anthropics/claude-quickstarts/autonomous-coding`, covered in 8.6.

**C compiler with a team of parallel Claudes (Feb 5, 2026, Nicholas Carlini)** — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler)
- *Scale:* **16 parallel Claude Opus 4.6 agents**, nearly **2,000 Claude Code sessions** over two weeks, **just under $20,000** in API cost, about **2B input and 140M output tokens**.
- *Result:* a roughly **100k-line** clean-room Rust C compiler. It builds Linux 6.9 on x86, ARM and RISC-V, plus QEMU, FFmpeg, SQLite, PostgreSQL and Redis, and passes about 99% of most compiler test suites, including the GCC torture tests.
- *Coordination had no orchestrator agent and no inter-agent messaging:*
  - A bash `while true` loop re-launches `claude` with a prompt file.
  - Each agent runs in its own Docker container, cloned from a bare git repo that acts as "upstream."
  - Agents claim tasks by writing a lock file to `current_tasks/`. A git push conflict forces the loser to pick another task.
  - Merge conflicts are frequent, and Claude resolves them itself.
  - Agents pick the "next most obvious" task.
- *Specialization by role:* one agent deduplicated code, one improved compiler performance, one improved generated-code efficiency, one critiqued the design as a Rust developer, one maintained docs.
- *Key failure and fix:* on one monolithic task (compiling the Linux kernel), all 16 agents hit the same bug and overwrote each other's fixes, so the extra agents did not help. The fix used **GCC as a known-good oracle**: compile most kernel files with GCC and a random subset with Claude's compiler, then delta-debug failing file pairs. That made the monolith parallelizable again.
- *Harness lessons:*
  - The verifier/test suite must be **nearly perfect**, or agents solve the wrong problem.
  - Keep test output to a few lines, send details to log files, and tag errors with `ERROR` so they are grep-able. This prevents context pollution. Precompute summary statistics.
  - A `--fast` mode runs a deterministic per-agent 1%/10% random sample to compensate for "time blindness."
  - CI was added late, after regressions kept happening.
  - Agents maintain READMEs and progress files because each one starts fresh.
  - One agent ran `pkill -9 bash` and killed its own loop.
- *Model progression:* Opus 4 barely produced a working compiler. Opus 4.5 passed test suites but could not build large projects. Opus 4.6 succeeded.

**Planner/generator/evaluator ("Harness design for long-running application development", Mar 24, 2026, Prithvi Rajasekaran)** — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps)
- *GAN-inspired split:* "Separating the agent doing the work from the agent judging it proves to be a strong lever." A standalone evaluator is easier to make skeptical than a generator is to make self-critical. Out of the box the evaluator still "talked itself out of real issues." It needed several rounds of prompt tuning against logs, plus few-shot calibration examples. "Claude out of the box is a poor QA agent."
- *Three agents:*
  - **Planner:** expands a 1–4 sentence prompt into a product spec, kept high level so spec errors do not cascade.
  - **Generator:** builds in sprints with git.
  - **Evaluator:** drives the running app with Playwright MCP and checks UI, API and database state against per-criterion hard thresholds. Failing any criterion fails the sprint.
- *Sprint contracts:* before each sprint, the generator proposes what it will build and how success will be verified. The evaluator reviews the proposal and they iterate to agreement. Sprint 3 alone had 27 criteria. Agents communicate **through files**.
- *Frontend-design variant:* four criteria (design quality, originality, craft, functionality), a few-shot-calibrated evaluator, Playwright MCP screenshots, 5–15 iterations, runs of up to 4 hours.
- *Numbers:*
  - RetroForge retro game maker on Opus 4.5: a solo run took **20 min / $9** and produced a broken game. The full harness took **6 hr / $200** (over 20x the cost) and produced 16 features across 10 sprints, playable.
  - Browser DAW on Opus 4.6 with a simplified harness: about **3 hr 50 min / $124.70** total. Planner 4.7 min / $0.46; build round 1 2 hr 7 min / $71.08; QA round 1 8.8 min / $3.24; build round 2 1 hr 2 min / $36.89; then two more short rounds. QA still caught stubbed features. "The builder ran coherently for over two hours without sprints."
- *Context resets* (fresh agent plus structured handoff artifact) were essential for Sonnet 4.5, which showed "context anxiety." With Opus 4.5 the behavior largely disappeared, so resets were dropped in favor of automatic compaction.
- *Simplify as models improve:* with Opus 4.6 the sprint construct was removed because the model "built coherently without decomposition," and the evaluator moved to a single end-of-run pass. The planner was kept, because without it the generator under-scoped the app. Components were removed one at a time to find which were load-bearing. "Every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own."

**Claude Code subagents (current docs)** — [Claude Code docs: subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents)
- The **Agent** tool was formerly the **Task** tool, and `Task(...)` still aliases it. Each subagent has its own context window, system prompt, tool allowlist and permissions, and **only the final report returns** to the parent. Claude delegates based on each agent's `description`.
- *Built-ins:* **Explore** (read-only; thoroughness quick/medium/very thorough; skips CLAUDE.md and git status), **Plan** (read-only, used in plan mode), **general-purpose** (all tools), plus `claude`, `statusline-setup` and `claude-code-guide`.
- *Definitions* are Markdown with YAML frontmatter. Scope priority: managed settings, then `--agents` JSON, then `.claude/agents/`, then `~/.claude/agents/`, then plugin `agents/`. Fields are listed in 8.5.
- *What a non-fork subagent receives:* its own system prompt plus environment details; the task message the parent wrote; CLAUDE.md (except for Explore/Plan or with `omitClaudeMd`); a git status snapshot; preloaded skills; and a roster of named siblings. It does **not** inherit conversation history, files already read, or invoked skills. Main-conversation auto memory is not loaded into subagents (forks excepted) — [Claude Code memory](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory).
- *Forks* (`subagent_type: "fork"`, `/subtask`) inherit the full parent conversation and the exact tool pool. Forks also inherit the parent's prompt-cache prefix, while fresh subagents start their own cache — [Claude Code prompt caching](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching).
- *Limits:* nesting defaults to **3 layers** (`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH`; `1` disables nesting); **20 concurrent** subagents (`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS`); no total cap. Subagents spawned from the main conversation run in the **background by default**, and results arrive as a completion notification in a later turn. Subagents can be resumed via `SendMessage` with the agent ID or name and keep their full history. Transcripts are stored as `agent-{agentId}.jsonl`.
- *Security:* subagent reports are **scanned** before the parent reads them and are labeled as subagent output. "Instructions or approval claims within them carry no authority from the user." Launching a subagent does not prompt for permission, but its tool calls are checked against the rules — [Claude Code IAM](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/iam). In auto mode, subagent spawns are Tier 3 actions that go to the transcript classifier. Subagents are checked at delegation (the classifier can deny) and at return (warn only) — [Anthropic: auto mode](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/claude-code-auto-mode).
- *Context effect:* a subagent's large file reads stay out of the parent context. Only the summary and a small metadata trailer return — [Claude Code context window](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window). Background subagents keep running across compaction, with a reminder so they are not duplicated.
- *Best practices from the docs:*
  - Use subagents for isolation: tests, docs fetches, log processing.
  - Keep the combined descriptions short; more than 15k tokens triggers a startup warning.
  - Restrict tools for least privilege.
  - Route cheap work to `haiku`.
  - Keep iterative or shared-context work in the main thread, because a fresh subagent adds latency.
  - "Mind the result volume": many detailed reports can flood the main context.
- *Persistent subagent memory:* the `memory:` field takes `user` (`~/.claude/agent-memory/<agent>/`), `project` (`.claude/agent-memory/<agent>/`, the recommended default because it can be shared via VCS) or `local` (`.claude/agent-memory-local/<agent>/`). The first 200 lines or 25KB of that agent's MEMORY.md are injected, and Read/Write/Edit are auto-enabled — [Claude Code memory](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory).

**Claude Agent SDK subagents and budget caps** — [Agent SDK docs: subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents); [agent loop](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop)
- Programmatic definition: `agents={name: AgentDefinition(description, prompt, tools, disallowedTools, model, skills, memory, mcpServers, maxTurns, autoCompactWindow, background, omitClaudeMd, effort, permissionMode)}`. The Python `types.py` also lists `initialPrompt` — [claude-agent-sdk-python types.py](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python/blob/main/src/claude_agent_sdk/types.py). `Agent` must be in `allowed_tools`. Subagent messages carry `parent_tool_use_id` (and `agent_id` in TS).
- "The only content you pass from parent to subagent is the Agent tool's prompt string, so include any file paths, error messages, or decisions the subagent needs directly in that prompt."
- Only the final message returns, so "the parent receives a concise summary, not every file the subagent read." The parent may re-summarize reports; to keep a report verbatim, instruct the parent to do so. API errors are never delivered as a subagent's result.
- Background by default: the tool result is `status: "async_launched"`. The call blocks and returns `status: "completed"` when Claude needs the result next.
- *Spend, depth and concurrency caps:* `max_budget_usd`/`maxBudgetUsd` refuses new spawns with `Budget limit reached`, stops background subagents, and ends with `error_max_budget_usd` (Claude Code v2.1.217+). The budget is checked *after* each model response, so spend "can therefore pass the cap by up to the cost of that one response," plus whatever running subagents spend. Subagent spend counts toward the cap. `max_turns` and `max_budget_usd` both default to "No limit," and the docs say "Setting a budget is a good default for production agents." The depth and concurrency env vars also apply.
- **"Claude Opus 5 delegates to subagents more readily than earlier models."** On the `claude_code` preset with Opus 5, Claude Code adds a system-prompt line telling Claude not to call the Agent tool unless asked. Custom prompts must add their own delegation instruction, and hard limits should be set regardless.
- The TS SDK exposes the `Workflow` tool from v0.3.149+.

**Claude Code agent teams (experimental)** — [Claude Code docs: agent teams](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams)
- Enabled with `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`. Components: a **team lead**; **teammates**, each a full independent Claude Code session; a **shared task list** (pending/in-progress/completed, with dependencies and auto-unblocking; **claiming uses file locking**); and a **mailbox** of JSON files at `~/.claude/teams/{team}/inboxes/{agent}.json`. Teammates message each other directly via `SendMessage`. Interactive sessions only; not available in `-p` or the Agent SDK. The release date was not found in the docs.
- *Subagents vs teams:* subagents report results to the caller, cost fewer tokens, and are coordinated by the main agent. Teammates are fully independent, coordinate themselves, and cost more because each is a separate instance.
- *Guidance:*
  - Start with **3–5 teammates**; "three focused teammates often outperform five scattered ones."
  - Aim for **5–6 tasks per teammate**, sized as self-contained deliverables.
  - **Avoid file conflicts** by giving each teammate its own file set; "two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites."
  - Start with research and review before parallel implementation.
  - The lead sometimes starts implementing instead of waiting, or stops early, so steer it.
  - Teammates "don't inherit the lead's conversation history," so spawn prompts must carry task-specific details. Example: "The app uses JWT tokens stored in httpOnly cookies. Report any issues with severity ratings."
- *Quality gates via hooks:* `TeammateIdle`, `TaskCreated` and `TaskCompleted`. Exit code 2 blocks the action and sends feedback, for example to enforce tests or lint before a task is accepted. Teammates in plan mode send plan-approval requests to the lead.
- *Recommended patterns:* parallel code review where each reviewer gets a distinct lens (security, performance, tests), and "competing hypotheses" debugging where 5 teammates try to disprove each other's root-cause theories, to counter anchoring.
- *Failure behavior:* a teammate that ends on an API error notifies the lead with the error text. Teammates may stop early after errors; the remedy is to re-instruct them or spawn a replacement.
- *Security:* teammate messages cannot approve permissions or relay a denied action. In auto mode, a classifier reviews inter-agent messages and treats relayed approval claims as untrusted.
- *Limitations:* no nested teams; one team per session; the lead is fixed; task status can lag and block dependents; in-process teammates are not restored on `/resume`; inter-agent messages cannot grant permissions.

**Claude Code dynamic workflows (introduced around May 28, 2026, v2.1.154+ per secondary sources)** — [Claude Code docs: workflows](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows); date and version from [agentic-ai docs mirror](https://agentic-ai.readthedocs.io/en/latest/WorkflowBuilders/dynamic-workflows/) and [alexop.dev](https://alexop.dev/posts/claude-code-workflows-deterministic-orchestration)
- Claude writes a **JavaScript orchestration script** that a background runtime executes. The script holds the loop, the branching and the intermediate results in variables, so "Claude's context holds only the final answer." Workflows can be saved (`.claude/workflows/`), parameterized via `args`, rerun, and resumed in the same session.
- *Script API:* `agent(prompt, {schema, label, stallMs, model…})`, `parallel()`, `pipeline(items, fn)`, `phase()`, `log()`, and an `args` global. `schema` forces JSON output, validated with up to 5 retries (`MAX_STRUCTURED_OUTPUT_RETRIES`). `agent()` resolves to `null` on stop or unrecoverable error.
- *Comparison from the docs:* subagents are "a few delegated tasks per turn"; agent teams are "a handful of long-running peers"; workflows are "dozens to hundreds of agents per run" and "resumable in the same session."
- *Limits:* **16 concurrent agents** by default (`CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS`, range 1–256); **4,096 items** per `parallel()`/`pipeline()`; **1,000 agents per run**; no mid-run user input; no filesystem access from the script itself; no `import()`.
- *Determinism and resume:* `Date.now()`, `Math.random()` and `new Date()` throw inside scripts, so a relaunch repeats the same `agent()` calls. Completed agents return cached results up to the first agent whose prompt differs; that agent and every later one re-run.
- *Fault handling:* a stalled agent auto-restarts up to 5 times (`stallMs`, `CLAUDE_ASYNC_AGENT_STALL_TIMEOUT_MS`). Inside `parallel`/`pipeline`, a failure leaves `null` and the run continues. A directly awaited failure ends the run. Usage-limit hits pause and auto-resume.
- *Cost controls:* a "Large workflow" warning fires above **25 agents or 1.5M projected tokens**. Size guideline values: `small` under 5, `medium` under 10 (default), `large` under 50 agents. "Run the workflow on a small slice first."
- *Prompt-cache sharing in fan-out:* agents with an identical model/effort/tools/schema/cwd prefix share cache. The runtime holds siblings until the first response begins (`CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS`, default 5000). The API reason: a cache entry becomes available only once the first response starts — [Claude prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching). Subagent cache TTL defaults to 5 minutes; `subagentPromptCacheTtl: 1h` extends it at a higher write cost.
- *Built-in quality patterns:* adversarial cross-review of findings before reporting; drafting a plan from several angles; "keep fixing until the type check passes or two rounds in a row make no progress"; "stop once two rounds in a row find nothing new." The bundled `/deep-research` workflow fans out searches, cross-checks sources, **votes on each claim**, and filters out claims that do not survive. Claims that cannot be checked are labeled unverified, not refuted. Other documented examples: per-file reviewers merged into one ranked summary, and a 500-file migration with "each file in its own isolated copy."
- *`ultracode` effort mode* lets Claude plan a workflow for every substantive task. A single request can become "one to understand the code, one to make the change, and one to verify it," at higher token cost.
- Practitioner advice: use workflows for repeatable, large-scale jobs (bug sweeps, migrations), and normal sessions or subagents for small, sequential work — [alexop.dev](https://alexop.dev/posts/claude-code-workflows-deterministic-orchestration).

**Related Anthropic loop surfaces**
- `/goal <condition>` (up to 4,000 characters) is "a wrapper around a session-scoped prompt-based Stop hook." After each turn a small fast model gets the condition plus the transcript and returns Not yet met, Met, or Impossible. The evaluator "does not call tools, so it can only judge what Claude has already surfaced." If background subagents or shells are running, evaluation is deferred, with check-ins after 30 minutes, then 1 h, then every 2 h, capped at three idle check-ins (`CLAUDE_CODE_GOAL_CHECKIN_MINUTES`) — [Claude Code /goal](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/goal).
- The hook type `agent` runs a subagent with tools as a hook (experimental; up to 50 tool-use turns; 60 s default timeout). `SubagentStart`/`SubagentStop`, `TaskCreated`/`TaskCompleted`, `TeammateIdle` and `WorktreeCreate`/`WorktreeRemove` are hook events — [Claude Code hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks).
- Scheduling surfaces: `/loop` (local interval), `/schedule` and "routines" (cloud; cron, API or GitHub events), and dynamic workflows — [Loop engineering](https://claude.com/blog/getting-started-with-loops).
- Managed Agents (Apr 8, 2026) splits session (append-only event log), harness and sandbox, so a crashed harness resumes via `wake(sessionId)` "from the last event." This is the durability substrate that long multi-agent runs need — [Anthropic: Managed Agents](https://anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents).
- The cookbook has `patterns/agents/` (workflows, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer, async multi-agent) and `claude_agent_sdk/` notebooks 00–08 (research, chief-of-staff, observability, SRE, migrating from the OpenAI Agents SDK, session browser, hosting, dynamic workflows) — [claude-cookbooks](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-cookbooks/tree/main/patterns/agents).

**What Anthropic's trajectory implies for a harness roadmap (inference):** (a) default to one strong agent; (b) add read-only, context-isolated subagents for search and verification; (c) separate generator and evaluator for quality; (d) use code-driven fan-out (workflows) for large homogeneous jobs; (e) use peer swarms only with a near-perfect external verifier and a file-level work partition.

#### OpenAI

The OpenAI Agents SDK formalizes two composition primitives, handoffs and agents-as-tools, and recommends code-driven orchestration when predictability matters. Codex runs parallel cloud tasks and subagents through a native multi-agent tool set. AgentKit's visual Agent Builder is reportedly being deprecated in 2026 in favor of the code-first SDK (secondary sources, conflicting dates). The notes contain no primary OpenAI multi-agent research paper from 2025–2026 comparable to Anthropic's posts.

**Agents SDK orchestration** — [OpenAI Agents SDK docs (multi_agent.md)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/openai-agents-python/main/docs/multi_agent.md)
- *Two orchestration modes.* **Via LLM:** an agent with instructions, tools and handoffs plans autonomously. The docs' tactics are good prompts, monitoring, self-critique loops, specialized agents over general ones, and evals. **Via code:** "more deterministic and predictable, in terms of speed, cost and performance."
- *Named code-orchestration patterns* (examples in `examples/agent_patterns`):
  - structured outputs to classify the task and pick the next agent
  - chaining (research → outline → draft → critique → revise)
  - an evaluator loop: a task agent runs in a `while` loop with an evaluator agent until the criteria pass
  - parallel independent agents via `asyncio.gather`
- **Agents as tools** (`Agent.as_tool()`): the manager keeps control. Best when one agent should own the final answer, combine specialist outputs, or enforce shared guardrails.
- **Handoffs:** a triage agent routes, and the specialist becomes the active agent for the rest of the turn. Best when the specialist should respond directly or routing is part of the workflow. Handoffs are exposed to the model as tools named `transfer_to_{agent.name}` — [handoffs/__init__.py](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/src/agents/handoffs/__init__.py). The two combine; for example, a triage agent hands off to a specialist that calls other agents as tools.
- *Run loop:* `Runner.run()` / `run_sync()` / `run_streamed()`. Each turn the output is classified as final output, a **handoff** (switch agent and input, then rerun) or tool calls. Handoffs are a third output class next to final output and tool calls. `max_turns` overflow raises `MaxTurnsExceeded` (`max_turns=None` disables it). `error_handlers` keys `"max_turns"`, `"model_refusal"` and `"invalid_final_output"` can return fallback outputs. `ToolExecutionConfig.max_function_tool_concurrency` caps parallel tool execution. A paused run resumes from a `RunState` — [running_agents.md](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/docs/running_agents.md).
- *Third-party rule of thumb:* "if the specialist owns the answer, handoff; if the manager owns the answer, tool." With handoffs, debugging misrouting requires understanding the routing logic, and choosing what history to filter on handoff "is a real design problem" — [team400.ai guide (Apr 2026)](https://team400.ai/blog/2026-04-openai-agent-orchestration-handoffs-guide); consistent with the [official JS multi-agent guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/multi-agent) (snippet only).
- *Guardrails:* `InputGuardrail` and `OutputGuardrail` return `GuardrailFunctionOutput(tripwire_triggered=…)`, and a tripwire halts execution — [guardrail.py](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/src/agents/guardrail.py). Tool-level guardrails live in `tool_guardrails.py`. Approval pauses the run, with `ToolApprovalItem`s in `RunResult.interruptions` (secondary). A vendor claims guardrails do not cover hosted tools, MCP, or computer/shell (vendor claim, unverified) — [Arcjet](https://arcjet.com/compare/openai-agents-guardrails-vs-arcjet).
- *Tracing:* built in and on by default. Each run records model calls, tool calls, handoffs, guardrails and custom spans in the Traces dashboard. A `withTrace` helper groups multiple runs into one trace, and trace processors export to Braintrust and others — [OpenAI Agents observability](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents/integrations-observability); code in `src/agents/tracing` — [tracing/](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/src/agents/tracing). OpenAI trace grading assigns structured scores to end-to-end traces; "Trace grading is the fastest way to identify workflow-level issues" — [OpenAI agent-evals guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agent-evals).
- *Durability:* the Temporal integration (public preview 2025-07-30, GA 2026-03-23) runs agents inside a Temporal Workflow, with each model invocation as an Activity. It is enabled with `OpenAIAgentsPlugin`, and `activity_as_tool` exposes Activities as durable tools. Demos include multi-agent interactive research — [Temporal blog](https://temporal.io/blog/announcing-openai-agents-sdk-integration); [demos](https://github.com/temporal-community/openai-agents-demos).
- *Memory for subagents:* `Memory(generate=None)` gives a read-only memory for subagents, checkers and one-off tool agents. Isolation is by `MemoryLayoutConfig`, not agent name — [sandbox memory](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/docs/sandbox/memory.md).
- *Not verified this session (openai.github.io blocked):* guardrail details beyond the source files, tracing span types, `handoff_input_filter`/`nest_handoff_history`, and Sessions semantics for handoffs.

**Codex multi-agent** — [openai/codex](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/main/codex-rs)
- Multi-agent tool names in the handler specs: `spawn_agent`, `send_input`, `send_message`, `wait_agent`, `close_agent`, `resume_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, `list_agents`, `followup_task`. The handler directory lists `multi_agents` and `multi_agents_v2` — [core/src/tools/handlers](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/main/codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers).
- Workspace crates include `agent-roles`, `message-board` and `worktree`. The `worktree` crate implies git worktrees isolate parallel tasks; this is inferred from the crate name only — [codex-rs tree](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/main/codex-rs). Tool plumbing has `orchestrator.rs` and `parallel.rs` under `core/src/tools/`.
- The Codex app for macOS launched **Feb 2, 2026** as a "command center" for managing multiple coding agents in parallel. Codex also spawns parallel subagents and consolidates their results — [IntuitionLabs (secondary)](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/openai-codex-app-ai-coding-agents); [heise](https://heise.de/-11165126). A claimed "5–7x for read-heavy tasks" speedup could not be verified.
- *Reviewer subagents:* `ApprovalsReviewer` is `user` (default) or `auto_review` (alias `guardian_subagent`). The guardian module "hosts approval decisions and the isolated synchronous reviewer" — [codex core/src/guardian](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/main/codex-rs/core/src/guardian).
- *Constrained background subagent:* the memory pipeline's Phase 2 spawns an internal **consolidation sub-agent** with no approvals, no network, local writes only, and no recursive delegation. Phase 1 extracts per rollout in parallel; Phase 2 serializes updates to shared artifacts under a single global lock. The pipeline never runs for sub-agent sessions — [codex memories README](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/memories/README.md).
- *Handoff-ready plans:* Plan Mode allows only non-mutating actions and ends in a `<proposed_plan>` that must be "decision complete" so another agent can implement it — [plan.md template](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/collaboration-mode-templates/templates/plan.md).
- *Thread operations relevant to orchestration:* CLI `fork`, `review`, `resume` and `cloud`; app-server `thread/fork`, `turn/steer`, `turn/interrupt` and `review/start` — [cli/src/main.rs](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/cli/src/main.rs); [app-server-protocol](https://github.com/openai/codex/tree/main/codex-rs/app-server-protocol). The hooks crate emits `SubagentStop` under the same name Claude Code uses.

**Swarm and AgentKit/Agent Builder**
- Swarm: "Swarm is now replaced by the OpenAI Agents SDK … We recommend migrating to the Agents SDK for all production use cases." It is described as "experimental, educational," client-side and stateless — [swarm README](https://github.com/openai/swarm/blob/main/README.md).
- Agent Builder, AgentKit's visual canvas launched at DevDay in Oct 2025, reportedly received deprecation notices on **June 3, 2026**, with shutdown cited as **Nov 30, 2026**. Sources disagree on the dates — [osher.com.au (secondary)](https://osher.com.au/blog/openai-agentkit/); [timewell.jp (secondary)](https://timewell.jp/en/columns/agent-builder). If accurate, visual low-code multi-agent canvases lost to code-first SDKs for production.
- Agent RFT (launched with AgentKit, Oct 2025) allows custom tool calls during RL rollouts. In practice, training reduced turns and models learned to issue more parallel calls — [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/presentations/rft-openai-model/).

**GPT-5 Pro / GPT-5.x Pro:** the notes found no primary source confirming a parallel multi-agent architecture. One weak source claims "scaled parallel compute… multiple reasoning shards… aggregating results" — [Ken Huang Substack (weak)](https://kenhuangus.substack.com/p/frontier-ai-models-technical-deep).

**Convergence with Anthropic (inference):** (1) a manager/agents-as-tools pattern for bounded subtasks where one agent owns the answer; (2) handoffs only for routing or triage-style UX; (3) code-level orchestration (gather, loops, structured routing) when cost and latency predictability matter.

#### DeepSeek

No public information in the research notes on DeepSeek multi-agent orchestration, agent swarms, or "heavy"/parallel-thinking agent modes. Searches returned only Kimi material. Adjacent facts that matter if DeepSeek models serve as workers in a multi-agent harness:
- DeepSeek-V3.2's search-agent RL data was built with a multi-agent pipeline that samples long-tail entities from web corpora and validates the generated QA pairs (data synthesis, not runtime orchestration) — [DeepSeek-V3.2 paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.02556) (via snippet).
- V3.2 discards historical reasoning content only when a new user message arrives. Harnesses that relay tool results or worker outputs as user messages trigger the discard. Tool-loop requests reportedly must pass `reasoning_content` back or the API returns 400 (secondary) — [DeepSeek API docs: Thinking Mode](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/thinking_mode/). V3.2-Speciale did not support tool calling.
- The Anthropic-compatible endpoint (`https://api.deepseek.com/anthropic`) reportedly maps `claude-opus*` to `deepseek-v4-pro`, and `claude-sonnet*`/`claude-haiku*` and unknown names to `deepseek-v4-flash` (search-summarized). In Claude Code, a subagent's `model: haiku` routing therefore lands on V4-Flash — [api-docs.deepseek.com anthropic_api](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/anthropic_api).

#### Open source and others

**Cognition (Devin)**
- *"Don't Build Multi-Agents" (June 2025, Walden Yan):* context engineering, not agent count, drives reliability. Principle 1: share full context and full agent traces, not just messages. Principle 2: actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions produce bad results. In the Flappy Bird example, two subagents (background and bird) build mismatched pieces because they lack each other's context. Recommendation: single-threaded linear agents, plus an LLM that compresses history for long tasks. The original was blocked; summarized via [jxnl.co](https://jxnl.co/writing/2025/09/11/why-cognition-does-not-use-multi-agent-systems/), the [agentic-ai docs summary](https://agentic-ai.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ContextEngineering/devin/) and search snippets (secondary).
- *"Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working" (April 2026), from search snippets:* "Most multi-agent setups in the world are limited to 'readonly' subagents... these mostly resemble tool calls rather than true multi-agent collaboration." Devin and Devin Review iterate against each other, and Devin Review catches **about 2 bugs per PR on Devin-written PRs, about 58% severe**. "The coding agent and review agent do not share any context beforehand," and "having a clean context makes the agent smarter because of the math of attention" — [Cognition blog (snippet)](https://cognition.com/blog/multi-agents-working); [X article](https://x.com/walden_yan/article/2047054401341370639).
- Secondary summaries say Yan holds that the 2025 warnings still apply to **parallel-writer swarms**, and that the working pattern is multiple agents contributing intelligence with **single-threaded writes**. This phrasing is unconfirmed against the original. Cognition also describes a lead/executor split: a frontier lead for planning and review and a cheaper executor such as SWE-2 — [AGNT summary](https://agnt.gg/articles/engineering/single-agent-vs-multi-agent); [ai.engineer (snippet)](https://ai.engineer/orgs/cognition).
- LangChain's response (snippet only): even read-heavy multi-agent systems need sophisticated context engineering, and write-heavy multi-agent is harder — [LangChain blog](https://blog.langchain.com/how-and-when-to-build-multi-agent-systems).

**Google**
- *ADK (community sources only):* `SequentialAgent` (deterministic pipeline); `ParallelAgent` (concurrent sub-agents writing to shared `session.state`, which need distinct `output_key`s); `LoopAgent` (runs until `escalate=True` or `max_iterations`); `AgentTool` (a specialist called as a function, with the result returned inline) versus sub-agent transfer (`transfer_to_agent`). Built-in MCP and A2A support — [community ADK guide](https://zack.onrender.com/docs/GEN%20AI%20DEV/Agents/Google%20ADK); [Google Cloud blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/build-multi-agentic-systems-using-google-adk); [nexu.io](https://nexu.io/blog/microsoft-agent-framework-maf-semantic-kernel-autogen).
- *Gemini CLI* (~108.7k stars, `v0.66.0`): built-in subagents (`codebase-investigator`, `generalist-agent`, `cli-help-agent`), remote agents over A2A (`a2a-client-manager.ts`), an `a2a-server` package, and an `agents.toml` policy profile — [core/src/agents](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/tree/main/packages/core/src/agents); [policies](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/tree/main/packages/core/src/policy/policies).
- *Scaling study* (with DeepMind and MIT, Dec 2025): see 8.3 counter-evidence and 8.4.
- *A2A:* donated to the Linux Foundation in June 2025 (launched under LF on Jun 23, 2025). The latest release is 1.0.0; v1.0 shipped around Mar–Apr 2026 (sources disagree: "March 2026 GA" vs "RC"), with v1.0.1 around May 2026. v1.0 adds signed Agent Cards, multi-tenancy, multi-protocol bindings with version negotiation, and the AP2 payments extension. Each server publishes an Agent Card at `/.well-known/agent-card.json` listing name, skills, interfaces, capabilities and security schemes. Bindings: JSON-RPC 2.0/HTTPS, gRPC, HTTP+JSON/REST. Some docs still show `A2A-Version: 0.3` headers. It joined AAIF (reported Aug 2026) — [A2A spec (via search summary)](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/); [AAIF blog](https://aaif.io/blog/a2a-joins-aaif); [letsdatascience (secondary)](https://letsdatascience.com/news/a2a-solidifies-cross-vendor-agent-interoperability-53400ea4); [tyk.io](https://tyk.io/blog/a2a-protocol/); [olostep](https://www.olostep.com/blog/a2a-protocol-agent2agent); [dev.to](https://dev.to/eclaw/a2a-protocol-tech-update-20260316-4fii).

**Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0** (around Apr 2–7, 2026; sources differ) — [Visual Studio Magazine](https://visualstudiomagazine.com/articles/2026/04/06/microsoft-ships-production-ready-agent-framework-1-0-for-net-and-python.aspx); [Microsoft devblog](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/agent-framework/?p=5212); [techstrong.ai](https://techstrong.ai/features/microsoft-ships-agent-framework-1-0-a-production-ready-foundation-for-multi-agent-ai/)
- Unifies Semantic Kernel and AutoGen. The stable surface is a single-agent abstraction, connectors, middleware hooks, memory/context providers and **graph-based workflows**, for .NET and Python.
- MCP for tools and A2A for interop. The A2A client and hosting packages moved to the A2A v1 SDK but are **still in preview**.
- Analyst caution: production constraints (latency, cost, observability) "reveal themselves only in live deployments."

**Moonshot (Kimi)**
- *Kimi K2.5 Agent Swarm* (research preview/beta on Kimi.com, early 2026): self-directs up to **100 sub-agents** across up to **1,500 coordinated steps or tool calls** (units differ across sources). A **trainable orchestrator** decomposes the task, and **dynamically instantiated frozen sub-agents** execute; "No predefined subagents or workflow." **PARL** (Parallel-Agent RL) addresses "**serial collapse**," where the orchestrator defaults to single-agent execution. An auxiliary reward encourages parallelism early, then shifts to task success, which prevents "fake parallelism." Latency is measured in "**critical steps**," so spawning helps only if it shortens the critical path. Reported gains: up to **4.5x** less execution time than a single agent, and **80%** lower end-to-end runtime in internal evals — [Kimi K2.5 blog (via snippet)](https://kimi.com/en/blog/kimi-k2-5); [techloy](https://www.techloy.com/moonshot-ais-kimi-k2-5-deploys-100-sub-agents-simultaneously-cuts-coding-time-by-4-5x/); [morphllm (third-party)](https://www.morphllm.com/kimi-k2-5-agent-swarm). No BrowseComp/WideSearch swarm-vs-single numbers or PARL reward formulas were obtained.
- *Kimi K2.6* reportedly raises this to **300 sub-agents and 4,000 steps** — [DataCamp (secondary)](https://www.datacamp.com/ko/tutorial/kimi-k2-agent-swarm-guide).
- *Kimi Code* (`MoonshotAI/kimi-code`, TS, MIT) has built-in `coder`/`explore`/`plan` subagents — [README](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/kimi-code/blob/main/README.md).

**xAI Grok 4 Heavy** (July 2025, background): launches parallel reasoning agents that "work independently, then compare notes," at about 10x test-time compute. HLE **44.4%** (Heavy) vs **25.4%** (Grok 4); the two figures may reflect different tool settings. Pricing is reported inconsistently ($300/mo vs $60/mo) — [OfficeChai](https://officechai.com/miscellaneous/elon-musk-explains-how-grok4-heavy-xais-multi-agent-reasoning-model-works/); [DataCamp](https://www.datacamp.com/blog/grok-4) (secondary).

**Open-source harnesses with subagents** (all from repo READMEs and trees)
- **deepagents** (`langchain-ai/deepagents`, ~30.9k stars, `deepagents==0.7.32`, built on LangGraph): sub-agents with isolated context via `subagents.py` and `async_subagents.py` middleware, plus filesystem offload and summarization — [middleware](https://github.com/langchain-ai/deepagents/tree/main/libs/deepagents/deepagents/middleware).
- **OpenHands** (~92.5k stars): the main repo is now "Agent Canvas," a control center that runs OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Pi, OpenCode or any ACP agent. The Software Agent SDK (`v1.59.0`) has a `subagent` module and tools `delegate`, `task`, `child_conversation`, `ask_oracle` and `tom_consult`, plus a `critic` module and a `StuckDetector` — [openhands-tools](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/tree/main/openhands-tools/openhands/tools); [sdk](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/tree/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk).
- **OpenCode**: primary agents `build` and `plan`, a `general` subagent invoked as `@general`, and core modules `session/subagent-job.ts` and `worktree.ts` — [packages/core/src](https://github.com/sst/opencode/tree/dev/packages/core/src).
- **Qwen Code** (Gemini CLI fork, `v0.26.6`) markets "SubAgents, Agent Teams" — [README](https://github.com/QwenLM/qwen-code/blob/main/README.md).
- **Letta Code**: subagents (general-purpose, forked, recall) and a background reflection subagent between turns — [letta-code](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/main/README.md); [reflection-v2.md](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/blob/main/src/agent/subagents/builtin/reflection-v2.md).
- **Pi** (~119.6k stars) "skips features like sub-agents and plan mode" by design. Its high adoption suggests subagents can be add-ons rather than core — [pi README](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/README.md).
- **LangGraph** (supervisor/swarm libraries, durable execution), **CrewAI** (crews/flows), **DSPy** (multi-module optimization) and **smolagents** (managed agents) were not researched; the notes have no verified 2026 status for them. The notes also found no reliable 2026 survey of which frameworks production teams use.

**Academic and independent studies** (details in 8.3 and 8.4): MAST (UC Berkeley, NeurIPS 2025); Google/DeepMind/MIT scaling (arXiv 2512.08296); single-agent-with-skills (arXiv 2601.04748); Tran and Kiela (arXiv 2604.02460); a clinical-workload MAS study (npj Health Systems 2026); debate studies (arXiv 2310.01798, 2509.05396, 2605.00914; ACL 2026 SRW); CodeMonkeys (arXiv 2501.14723).

### 8.3 Techniques and patterns

Production-proven patterns, roughly in order of evidence: (1) orchestrator-worker fan-out for breadth research; (2) generator/evaluator with a fresh-context, skeptical evaluator; (3) map-reduce over items with schema-constrained outputs and an adversarial verify/dedup stage; (4) swarms partitioned by file or task, coordinated by git, lock files and a near-perfect test oracle; (5) best-of-N or parallel rollouts with a selector. Each technique below gives what it is, mechanics, evidence, and when to use it.

**Deciding whether to go multi-agent (the decision rule)**
- *What:* a gate before any fan-out, informed by the controlled studies and practitioner cost data.
- *Mechanics:* go multi-agent only when all four hold. (1) The task decomposes into subtasks with low mutual dependency (breadth-first search, per-file audits, independent failing tests). (2) Each subtask's output can be checked or merged without re-deriving the other subtasks' context. (3) The single-agent baseline is weak, or its context use is already degraded. (4) The task value justifies 4–20x the token cost. Otherwise use one agent with good context engineering, skills and compaction (synthesized in the notes).
- *Evidence:*
  - Google Research/DeepMind/MIT (arXiv 2512.08296, Dec 2025; reported via snippets) compared 5 architectures (single-agent; independent, centralized, decentralized and hybrid multi-agent) across three LLM families, with 180 configurations in v1 and **260 configurations across 6 benchmarks** later. Multi-agent gave **+81% on Finance-Agent** (parallelizable), while **all multi-agent variants degraded sequential reasoning (PlanCraft) by 39–70%**. **Independent** agents amplified errors **17.2x**; **centralized** coordination contained errors best. **Capability saturation:** returns diminish or turn negative once the single-agent baseline exceeds about **45%**. A predictive model chose the optimal architecture for **87%** of unseen configurations — [arXiv 2512.08296](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.08296); [HF papers](https://huggingface.co/papers/2512.08296); [Google Research blog](https://research.google/blog/towards-a-science-of-scaling-agent-systems-when-and-why-agent-systems-work/).
  - MAST (Cemri et al., UC Berkeley, NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2503.13657): **14 failure modes** in **3 categories**: specification/system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification. v1 covered 5 frameworks and 150+ tasks, v2 7 frameworks and 200+ tasks, and v3 **1,642 MAS execution traces** — [arXiv (snippet)](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3); [NeurIPS 2025](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/122442). A secondary source reports category shares of specification/system design **44.2%** and task verification **23.5%** (so inter-agent misalignment is about 32%), and failure rates across studied systems of **41%–86.7%**, not comparable across benchmarks. These shares are unverified against the paper — [Antoine Buteau (secondary)](https://www.antoinebuteau.com/multi-agent-systems-fail-like-organizations/).
  - Tran and Kiela (arXiv 2604.02460, Apr 2026): at a fixed thinking-token budget, single agents match or beat MAS on multi-hop reasoning. MAS pulls ahead only when the single agent's context use is already degraded (reported) — [alphaXiv](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2604.02460v1); [beancount.io summary](https://beancount.io/bean-labs/research-logs/2026/05/31/single-agent-outperforms-multi-agent-equal-token-budget).
  - Contrary result: in a clinical-workload study (npj Health Systems 2026), single-agent accuracy degraded as batch size grew, while an orchestrated MAS held up and used up to **65x fewer tokens** — [BIDMC listing](https://research.bidmc.org/radiology-research/publications/orchestrated-multi-agents-sustain-accuracy-under-clinical-scale-workloads-compared).
  - Practitioner costs: about 15x chat tokens ([Anthropic research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)); over 20x for the full planner/generator/evaluator harness, which was nonetheless the only version that worked ($200 vs $9) ([Harness design](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps)); 16 agents gave zero benefit on a single shared bug until an oracle partitioned the work ([C compiler](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler)).
- *Use when:* breadth research, per-item audits, migrations, independent test failures, review. *Avoid when:* sequential planning, tightly coupled edits, or a strong single-agent baseline (above about 45%).

**Effort scaling in the lead prompt**
- *What:* explicit rules in the orchestrator prompt that map task complexity to agent count and tool-call budget.
- *Mechanics:* simple fact-finding uses 1 agent and 3–10 tool calls; direct comparisons use 2–4 subagents at 10–15 calls each; complex research uses more than 10 subagents with divided responsibilities. The lead spawns 3–5 at once, and each uses 3+ tools in parallel.
- *Evidence:* research time cut by up to 90% on complex queries — [Anthropic research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system). Without steering, models misjudge parallelism in both directions: Kimi's "serial collapse" and Opus 5's over-delegation.
- *Use when:* the LLM decides *whether* to fan out. Pair it with harness caps, because the prompt alone does not bound spend.

**Context-isolated read-only subagent**
- *What:* a fresh-context worker for large reads (codebase exploration, docs fetches, log processing, test runs) that returns a short summary.
- *Mechanics:* use a read-only tool allowlist (Claude Code's Explore skips CLAUDE.md and git status and offers quick/medium/very thorough levels). Return 1,000–2,000 tokens or a file reference. Route to a cheap model (`haiku`).
- *Evidence:* "Sub-agents explore with tens of thousands of tokens but return condensed summaries, often 1,000–2,000 tokens" — [Anthropic context engineering](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents). Cognition: most real-world multi-agent is "readonly" subagents that "mostly resemble tool calls" (snippet).
- *Use when:* exploration is large relative to the result. *Avoid when:* the work is iterative or needs shared context with the main thread, since a fresh subagent adds latency.

**Orchestrator-worker fan-out**
- *What:* a lead plans, writes explicit briefs, spawns parallel workers, synthesizes, then runs a specialized post-pass (for example citations).
- *Mechanics:* lead (Opus) saves the plan to memory, spawns 3–5 workers (Sonnet) per batch with interleaved thinking, decides whether more research is needed, and hands off to a CitationAgent. Workers write artifacts and return references.
- *Evidence:* +90.2% over single-agent Opus 4; about 15x tokens; synchronous batches are a bottleneck — [Anthropic research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system).
- *Use when:* breadth-first, read-heavy research with independent threads. *Avoid when:* "most coding tasks."

**Generator–evaluator (evaluator-optimizer) with sprint contracts**
- *What:* one agent builds; a separate, skeptical, fresh-context agent judges against hard criteria; the loop iterates.
- *Mechanics:* agree a criteria file (sprint contract) before work; have the evaluator exercise the running artifact end to end against hard per-criterion thresholds; calibrate it with few-shot examples and log-driven prompt tuning; on stronger models, collapse to one end-of-run pass (details in 8.2). The OpenAI equivalent is a task agent in a `while` loop with an evaluator agent. Claude Code's lightweight equivalent is `/goal`, where a small model judges the transcript at each stop attempt but cannot call tools.
- *Evidence:* the $200 / 6 hr harness was playable where the $9 / 20 min solo run was broken; QA still caught stubbed features in the DAW run — [Harness design](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps). Evaluator-optimizer also appears as Codex's goal "completion audit" ("The audit must prove completion, not merely fail to find obvious remaining work") — [codex ext/goal](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/ext/goal/templates/goals/continuation.md).
- *Use when:* criteria are clear and checkable, and iteration "provides measurable value" ([Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)). *Avoid when:* the evaluator cannot observe end state; a judge without tools "can only judge what Claude has already surfaced."

**Fresh-context reviewer**
- *What:* a second agent with no shared prior context reviews the first agent's output (PR, plan, findings).
- *Mechanics:* give the reviewer the artifact and criteria only, not the generator's reasoning; iterate generator against reviewer.
- *Evidence:* Devin Review catches about 2 bugs per PR on Devin-written PRs, about 58% severe; "having a clean context makes the agent smarter because of the math of attention" (snippet) — [Cognition](https://cognition.com/blog/multi-agents-working). "Use a separate reviewer agent with fresh context" — [Loop engineering](https://claude.com/blog/getting-started-with-loops).
- *Use when:* almost always for code changes; it is the cheapest high-yield second agent, because it avoids self-assessment bias and context bloat.

**Planner front-end**
- *What:* an agent that expands a short prompt into a high-level spec before building.
- *Mechanics:* turn a 1–4 sentence prompt into a product spec; stay high level so spec errors do not cascade. It cost 4.7 min / $0.46 in the DAW run.
- *Evidence:* kept even after other scaffolding was removed on Opus 4.6, because "without it the generator under-scoped" — [Harness design](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps). Codex Plan Mode produces a "decision complete" `<proposed_plan>` that another agent can implement.
- *Use when:* the prompt is under-specified and the build is long.

**Sequential multi-session handoff (initializer plus worker; context reset)**
- *What:* agents run one after another across fresh contexts, with state in files.
- *Mechanics:* the initializer writes `init.sh`, `claude-progress.txt`, an initial commit and an immutable JSON feature list (agents flip only `passes`). Each worker session runs a start ritual, does one feature, commits and updates progress. For models with "context anxiety," a context reset means a fresh agent plus a structured handoff artifact.
- *Evidence:* addressed one-shotting, premature victory and untested "done" marks — [Effective harnesses](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents). Resets were essential for Sonnet 4.5 and unnecessary for Opus 4.5+, where compaction sufficed — [Harness design](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/harness-design-long-running-apps).
- *Use when:* the work spans many context windows. Keep resets behind a per-model flag.

**Map-reduce / pipeline with schema outputs**
- *What:* apply the same agent template to many items, then one agent ranks and deduplicates.
- *Mechanics:* `pipeline(items, item => agent(prompt, {schema}))`, then a merge agent. Failed items become `null` and the run continues. Each item can run in an isolated copy.
- *Evidence:* documented examples are per-file reviewers merged into one ranked summary, and a 500-file migration with "each file in its own isolated copy" — [Claude Code workflows](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows).
- *Use when:* the job is homogeneous and per-item (reviews, migrations, bug sweeps). *Avoid when:* items depend on each other's results.

**Adversarial verification and claim voting**
- *What:* independent agents cross-check findings before they are reported; claims are voted on and filtered.
- *Mechanics:* `/deep-research` fans out searches, cross-checks sources, "votes on each claim," and drops claims that do not survive. Uncheckable claims are labeled unverified, not refuted. Workflows can "have independent agents adversarially review each other's findings before they're reported."
- *Evidence:* [Claude Code workflows](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows). Needed because independent agents without a checker amplify errors 17.2x (reported).
- *Use when:* any fan-out whose output is reported to a user.

**Iterate-until-convergence loops**
- *What:* repeat fix or find rounds until a check passes or progress stalls.
- *Mechanics:* "keep fixing until the type check passes or two rounds in a row make no progress"; "find issues until the list stops growing" / "stop once two rounds in a row find nothing new." Related guards: Codex's no-progress check and a blocked status only after the same blocker repeats for at least three consecutive goal turns; Claude Code overrides a Stop hook after it blocks eight times in a row with no tool call in between.
- *Evidence:* [Claude Code workflows](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows); [codex ext/goal](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/ext/goal/templates/goals/continuation.md); [Claude Code hooks guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide).
- *Use when:* the exit criterion is executable (type check, tests, finding count).

**Multi-lens parallel review**
- *What:* parallel reviewers, each with a distinct lens (security, performance, test coverage).
- *Mechanics:* identical inputs, different system prompts or criteria; merge and deduplicate findings with severity ratings.
- *Evidence:* recommended in [agent teams docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams) and the [Agent SDK docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents). Heterogeneous lenses are preferred over homogeneous debate (see below).
- *Use when:* reviewing a diff or design, where reviewers only read.

**Competing hypotheses**
- *What:* several agents each try to disprove the others' root-cause theories.
- *Mechanics:* 5 teammates, each owning one hypothesis and attacking the rest, to counter anchoring.
- *Evidence:* recommended pattern in [agent teams docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams); no quantitative result in the notes.
- *Use when:* debugging with an unclear root cause.

**Peer swarm with task locks (no orchestrator)**
- *What:* N identical agents, each in its own container, loop over "pick the next most obvious task," coordinated only by git.
- *Mechanics:* relaunch loop, per-agent container on a bare upstream, `current_tasks/` lock files arbitrated by git push conflicts, self-resolved merge conflicts, role-specialized agents, agent-maintained READMEs and progress files, and CI as a regression gate (full protocol under Anthropic in 8.2).
- *Evidence:* 16 agents, about 2,000 sessions, under $20,000, a 100k-line compiler that builds Linux 6.9 — [C compiler](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler).
- *Use when:* there is a nearly perfect verifier and the work partitions into many independent tasks. *Avoid when:* the work is one monolithic task (all 16 agents hit the same bug) unless it can be partitioned with an oracle.

**Oracle-based partitioning of a monolith**
- *What:* use a known-good reference implementation to turn one big failing task into many independent ones.
- *Mechanics:* compile most kernel files with GCC and a random subset with the agent's compiler; delta-debug failing file pairs so each failure is a separate, attributable task.
- *Evidence:* restored parallelism on the Linux kernel build — [C compiler](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler).
- *Use when:* any reference oracle exists (old implementation, other compiler, golden outputs).

**One-writer rule ("many readers or critics, one writer")**
- *What:* any number of agents may read, search, review or propose, but writes to shared state go through one agent at a time.
- *Mechanics:* readers and reviewers get read-only tools. One integrator (the lead or a merge agent) owns the main branch. Parallel writers are allowed only with strict partitioning (file ownership, worktrees, task locks) **and** an external oracle (tests, compiler, CI). The single-agent loop applies the same rule internally: read-only tools (`Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`, read-only MCP) run concurrently, while state-modifying tools (`Edit`, `Write`, `Bash`) run sequentially, and custom tools are sequential unless they set `readOnlyHint` — [agent loop docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop).
- *Evidence:* Cognition's "single-threaded writes" (secondary); Flappy Bird mismatch; "two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites" — [agent teams](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams); the 16-agent overwrite failure; Codex memory Phase 2 serializing writes under a global lock.
- *Use when:* always, as the default write policy.

**Worktree or container per writer**
- *What:* each parallel writer gets its own checkout.
- *Mechanics:* `isolation: worktree` runs a Claude Code subagent in a temporary git worktree. `WorktreeCreate`/`WorktreeRemove` hooks exist. Codex has a `worktree` crate (inferred), and OpenCode has `worktree.ts`. The C compiler used one Docker container per agent cloned from a bare upstream. Checkpoints should snapshot Bash side effects too (git-stash or worktree snapshots), since SDK checkpoints miss Bash edits.
- *Evidence:* the notes found no rigorous public benchmark of N worktree agents vs 1 with quality and merge-conflict rates.
- *Use when:* more than one agent writes code. Combine with a shared test oracle, a CI gate before merge, and a single integrator.

**File, mailbox and blackboard communication**
- *What:* agents coordinate through durable files instead of conversation.
- *Mechanics:* shared task list with dependencies and file-locked claiming; JSON mailboxes at `~/.claude/teams/{team}/inboxes/{agent}.json`; progress files; JSON feature lists; sprint-contract files; artifact paths returned from subagents. Google ADK's `ParallelAgent` branches write to shared `session.state` and need distinct `output_key`s.
- *Evidence:* used across every Anthropic system in the notes; Cognition's principle 1 ("share full context and full agent traces, not just messages") is the counter-argument for tasks needing shared context.
- *Use when:* agents run long or in parallel. Namespace keys per agent.

**Handoffs vs agents-as-tools**
- *What:* two ways to compose agents. With a handoff the active agent changes; with agent-as-tool a manager calls a specialist and keeps control.
- *Mechanics:* OpenAI `transfer_to_{agent.name}` vs `Agent.as_tool()`; ADK `transfer_to_agent` vs `AgentTool`; Claude Code subagents are agent-as-tool (only the final report returns).
- *Evidence:* "if the specialist owns the answer, handoff; if the manager owns the answer, tool" (third-party); history filtering on handoff "is a real design problem."
- *Use when:* handoffs for triage or routing UX; agents-as-tools for bounded subtasks, combining outputs or enforcing shared guardrails.

**Code-driven orchestration (deterministic workflows)**
- *What:* the plan lives in a script (loops, branches, variables), and the LLM is called per step.
- *Mechanics:* Claude Code workflows (`agent`/`parallel`/`pipeline`/`phase`, schema outputs, deterministic replay, banned nondeterminism, cached results for unchanged prefixes); OpenAI code orchestration (structured-output routing, chaining, evaluator loops, `asyncio.gather`). At the tool level, programmatic tool calling lets Claude write Python that calls tools via `asyncio.gather` inside code execution, so intermediate results never enter context.
- *Evidence:* programmatic tool calling cut average tokens from 43,588 to 27,297 (−37%) on complex research tasks — [Anthropic advanced tool use](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/advanced-tool-use). No published head-to-head of code-driven vs LLM-driven orchestration cost on the same task was found.
- *Use when:* the job is repeatable and large (dozens to hundreds of agents), or cost and latency predictability matter. Hybrid: the LLM decides *whether* to fan out, and a script runs the fan-out.

**Best-of-N / parallel test-time compute / heavy modes**
- *What:* N independent rollouts, then selection or aggregation.
- *Mechanics:* run N attempts (in isolated sandboxes for code), select with an executable verifier (tests) first and an LLM judge as tie-breaker, or have an aggregator read all N.
- *Evidence:* Sonnet 4.5 on SWE-bench Verified at 77.2% single vs **82.0% with parallel compute** (secondary table; sampling count undisclosed; internal scoring model) — [Verdent (secondary)](https://www.verdent.ai/guides/claude-sonnet-5-swe-bench-verified-results); [GreaterWrong discussion](https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/hmZHPE4ZJvEc3khgQ/checking-in-on-ai-2027/comment/LzyFabszAsB6b7sJm). Grok 4 Heavy HLE 44.4% vs 25.4% at about 10x compute (secondary). CodeMonkeys: **selection quality** is the bottleneck — [arXiv 2501.14723 (snippet)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.14723). MaTTS (memory-aware test-time scaling) on WebArena-Shopping: 49.7% → 55.1% (parallel, k=5) (memory notes).
- *Use when:* the task is verifiable and value is high. *Avoid when:* there is no good selector.

**Trained orchestration (PARL)**
- *What:* RL-train the orchestrator to decide when and how wide to spawn.
- *Mechanics:* frozen, dynamically instantiated sub-agents; an auxiliary parallelism reward early in training that shifts to task success; latency counted in critical steps.
- *Evidence:* up to 4.5x faster and 80% lower end-to-end runtime (reported) — Kimi K2.5.
- *Use when:* you train your own models. For a harness, adopt the "critical steps" metric (latency equals the longest dependent chain) as telemetry for whether a fan-out helped.

**Model tiering (lead and executor)**
- *What:* a frontier model plans and reviews; cheaper models execute.
- *Mechanics:* Opus lead with Sonnet workers; per-agent `model` (`haiku` for cheap work); Cognition's frontier lead with a cheaper executor such as SWE-2 (secondary). Keep the model and effort fixed within a cache-sharing sibling group, because switching model or effort breaks the cache.
- *Evidence:* [Anthropic research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system); cheaper subagent models are listed among production cost levers in the evals notes.

**Fork vs fresh context**
- *What:* a fork inherits the full parent conversation; a fresh subagent starts clean.
- *Mechanics:* Claude Code `subagent_type: "fork"` or `/subtask` (full history, exact tool pool, shared cache prefix) vs default subagents (task message only).
- *Evidence:* forks address Cognition's shared-context concern; fresh contexts suit independent review — [Claude Code subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents); [Cognition (snippet)](https://cognition.com/blog/multi-agents-working).
- *Use when:* fork for side tasks that need the conversation (and prefix-sharing side work such as compaction); fresh for review and unbiased exploration.

**Multi-agent debate (weak value per token)**
- *What:* homogeneous agents argue toward consensus.
- *Evidence:* equal-response debate does no better than majority voting; gains come from consistency, not self-correction ("LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet") — [arXiv 2310.01798](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.01798). "Talk Isn't Always Cheap" (2025) finds debate can make answers worse than a single agent's — [arXiv 2509.05396](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.05396v2). "The Cost of Consensus" (2026 preprint) reports **2.1–3.4x more tokens** than isolated self-correction for equal or lower accuracy — [arXiv 2605.00914 (snippet)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.00914). Contrary: ACL 2026 SRW "Multi-Agent Reasoning Improves Compute Efficiency" reports debate beats self-consistency by about 1.3 points on MMLU-Pro at equal compute, and self-consistency saturates earlier on hard tasks — [ACL Anthology preview](https://preview.aclanthology.org/ingest-acl/2026.acl-srw.1/).
- *Use instead:* independent sampling plus a verifier or vote, or heterogeneous critics with different lenses.

**Single agent with a skill library (the alternative to multi-agent)**
- *What:* compile a MAS into one agent that selects from skills.
- *Evidence:* matched MAS accuracy (+0.7% on average) with **54% fewer tokens and 50% lower latency**; selection accuracy **degrades sharply beyond about 50–100 skills**, and semantically similar skills make it worse (reported) — [arXiv 2601.04748 (snippet)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.04748).
- *Use when:* the "agents" differ mainly in instructions rather than in context needs. Keep the skill count under about 50 and descriptions distinct.

**Delegation brief (contract)**
- *What:* the self-contained task message a parent writes for a worker.
- *Mechanics:* objective, output format, tools and sources guidance, clear task boundaries, plus file paths, error messages and decisions the worker needs, because the prompt string is the only content passed. See the template in 8.7.
- *Evidence:* vague briefs caused duplication and gaps — [Anthropic research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system); "include any file paths, error messages, or decisions the subagent needs directly in that prompt" — [Agent SDK](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents).

**Condensed, schema or reference returns**
- *What:* bound what flows back to the parent.
- *Mechanics:* only the final message returns; a schema with validation and up to 5 retries (`MAX_STRUCTURED_OUTPUT_RETRIES`; the SDK's terminal subtype is `error_max_structured_output_retries`); artifact paths plus a short summary; an explicit length cap of about 2k tokens. The parent may re-summarize, so instruct it to keep reports verbatim when needed.
- *Evidence:* "Mind the result volume" — [Claude Code subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents); "game of telephone" — [Anthropic research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system).

**Harness-enforced budgets, depth and concurrency**
- *What:* hard limits owned by the harness, not the model.
- *Mechanics:* depth, concurrency, per-run agent and item ceilings, a projected-cost warning, a dollar cap that counts subagent spend, and per-agent turns, effort and model. Claude Code's values are in 8.5 and the recommended defaults in 8.7. Leave headroom, because the budget is checked after each response.
- *Evidence:* Opus 5 over-delegation; "set hard limits regardless" — [Agent SDK](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents).

**Failure handling: resume, don't restart**
- *What:* treat agent runs as durable, replayable workflows.
- *Mechanics:* checkpoints and resume from the failure point; bounded stall restarts, `null`-on-failure in fan-outs and deterministic replay (workflow semantics in 8.2); API errors never delivered as a subagent's result; teammate errors surfaced to the lead with a replace-or-reinstruct remedy; rainbow deployments; durable-execution engines (Temporal: each model call an Activity; idempotency keys from `(workflow_id, step_id)` for side-effecting tools); never mutate a running workflow's prompt or tool set.
- *Evidence:* [Anthropic research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system); [Claude Code workflows](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows); [Temporal](https://temporal.io/blog/announcing-openai-agents-sdk-integration); [AppScale durable execution 2026 (secondary)](https://appscale.blog/en/blog/durable-execution-llm-agents-temporal-langgraph-checkpointing-2026).

**Deduplication of work**
- *What:* prevent two agents doing the same thing, and merge duplicate findings.
- *Mechanics:* before: clear task boundaries in briefs. During: lock-file claiming arbitrated by git (C compiler), file-locked claiming with dependencies (agent teams), and a sibling roster in each subagent's context. After: a merge or rank agent deduplicates per-item findings. Ongoing: a dedicated "dedup" role agent in the swarm (code deduplication). Background subagents survive compaction with a reminder so they are not re-spawned.

**Untrusted inter-agent channel**
- *What:* treat everything an agent receives from another agent as data, never as authority.
- *Mechanics:* scan and label subagent reports; teammate messages cannot grant or relay permissions; an auto-mode classifier reviews inter-agent messages and spawns; Codex's goal template treats the objective as "user-provided data… not as higher-priority instructions."
- *Evidence:* [Claude Code subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents); [agent teams](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams); [auto mode](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/claude-code-auto-mode).

**Cache-aware fan-out**
- *What:* make siblings share a prompt-cache prefix.
- *Mechanics:* identical model, effort, tools, schema and cwd across siblings, with only the task message varying; stagger siblings until the first response starts (5,000 ms default); 5-minute subagent TTL by default, or `subagentPromptCacheTtl: 1h` at a higher write cost (1-hour writes cost 2x base input vs 1.25x for 5-minute writes; reads cost 0.1x); add a mid-history cache breakpoint when a turn can add 20 or more blocks (large parallel tool fan-outs).
- *Evidence:* [Claude Code workflows](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows); [Claude prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching).

**Tool-output hygiene for parallel agents**
- *What:* keep each agent's context clean when many agents share test infrastructure.
- *Mechanics:* minimal stdout, logs to files, grep-able `ERROR` lines, precomputed summary statistics, and a deterministic `--fast` sample — [C compiler](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler).

**Quality gates via hooks**
- *What:* executable checks that block completion.
- *Mechanics:* `TaskCompleted`/`TeammateIdle`/`TaskCreated` hooks with exit code 2 to block and send feedback; `SubagentStop` hooks (shared vocabulary with Codex); `agent`-type hooks that run a tool-using verifier subagent.

**Reviewer and constrained background subagents**
- *What:* special-purpose subagents with narrow powers.
- *Mechanics:* Codex `approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"` (`guardian_subagent`), an isolated synchronous reviewer for approvals; Claude Code's auto-mode transcript classifier, which runs on Sonnet 4.6 and sees only user messages and tool calls; Codex's memory consolidation sub-agent (no approvals, no network, local writes only, no recursive delegation); the Agents SDK's `Memory(generate=None)` read-only memory for subagents and checkers; Letta's background reflection subagent.
- *Use when:* the subagent's job is judgment or maintenance. Strip its powers to the minimum and forbid recursive delegation.

**A2A for cross-boundary agents**
- *What:* an HTTP-level protocol for independently deployed agents.
- *Mechanics:* Agent Card at `/.well-known/agent-card.json`; JSON-RPC 2.0, gRPC or REST bindings; signed cards in v1.0.
- *Use when:* crossing trust or organization boundaries (Gemini CLI remote subagents, Microsoft Agent Framework interop). *Avoid* for in-harness orchestration, where function calls, files and git are simpler.
